profiles.name: Albert Stangeland
profiles.query: "Albert Stangeland" IWW 1918 prisoner portrait photograph archive
profiles.identity_context: Albert Stangeland was an Industrial Workers of the World member from Chicago imprisoned by the US military during World War I. A prisoner letter published in the December 1919 One Big Union Monthly identifies him among the religious and political opponents of war held at Fort Douglas, Utah. It records his confinement at Camp Jackson, South Carolina, on August 9, 1918, and a court-martial sentence of fifty years for disobedience of orders under Article 64 of the Articles of War, approved September 17, 1918. The sentence was reduced to five years in April 1919. A separate prisoner directory in the March 1920 issue again lists him at Fort Douglas. His eventual release date has not been established.
profiles.finding: Identity-specific search reviewed; no adequately identified, usable portrait verified for deployment. Sources and returned evidence preserved in group search log; unresolved leads remain open.

profiles.name: Alice Cosu
profiles.query: "Alice Cosu" 1917 suffrage National Woman Party portrait photograph archive
profiles.identity_context: Alice Cosu was a New Orleans suffragist and Silent Sentinel. Arrested in 1917 picketing the Wilson White House for women's right to vote and sentenced to the Occoquan Workhouse in Virginia, where she was Alice Paul's cellmate and was subjected to the brutality of the November 14, 1917 "Night of Terror." Cosu suffered a heart attack from the conditions of her imprisonment and never fully recovered. She continued NWP organizing in Louisiana through the 19th Amendment's ratification.
profiles.finding: NWP finding aid identifies Alice Cosu correspondence. Dora Lewis photographs are not evidence of Cosu's face.

profiles.name: Elizabeth McShane
profiles.query: "Elizabeth McShane" 1917 suffrage National Woman Party portrait photograph archive
profiles.identity_context:
Elizabeth McShane was a member of the National Woman's Party and one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. She was jailed three times and hunger-struck in at least two of those terms. (November 9, 1891 - August 13, 1976; later Elizabeth McShane Hilles)

Arrested while picketing on November 10, 1917, she was sentenced on November 16 to fifteen days. She was sent first to the Occoquan Workhouse and then transferred to the District Jail, where she was FORCE-FED during a hunger strike. She was released on November 27, eleven days after sentencing.

Arrested again on August 6, 1918 during the Lafayette Square demonstration, she was released and then convicted, and was committed about August 15 to the old District Workhouse on a fifteen-day sentence. She was released on August 20 after a hunger strike, roughly five days into the term.

Arrested a third time on February 9, 1919 at the final watchfire demonstration, she was sentenced on February 10 to five days in the District Jail and released on February 13.

Stevens's appendix dates that last term to January. The chronological narrative in Irwin and the Library of Congress detailed chronology both place it in February, and this record follows them.
profiles.finding: Named sixth from left in NWP reel173 frame78 group. Original image and clean crop pending.

profiles.name: Josephine Bell
profiles.query: "Josephine Bell" Masses poet 1917 portrait photograph archive
profiles.identity_context: Josephine Bell was a Poet and Masses contributor. Indicted in November 1917 along with editor Max Eastman, John Reed, and the staff of The Masses — the radical New York socialist literary magazine — under the Espionage Act of 1917 for conspiracy to obstruct military recruitment. The Post Office had already revoked the magazine's second-class mailing privileges, effectively shutting it down. The first trial (April 1918) and second trial (October 1918) both ended in hung juries; the government declined a third prosecution and the charges were dismissed. The Masses re-emerged as The Liberator under Eastman's editorship. Bell was indicted specifically over her poem "A Tribute" — a sympathetic verse about jailed anarchist anti-conscription organizers Alexander Berkman and Emma Goldman published in The Masses; the indictment quoted her poem as proof of conspiracy to obstruct the draft. Charges dismissed against her with the rest of the defendants.
profiles.finding: British crime writer born1897 rejected as unsupported match for Masses poet.
